\section{Setting and method}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Setting.}
A benchmark has $N$ items.
A \emph{target} model has an unknown binary vector $y\in\{0,1\}^N$ ($y_j=1$ if it answers item $j$ correctly) and a full-benchmark score $\mu=\frac1N\sum_j y_j$ that we want to know without running all items.
We hold the results $Y\in\{0,1\}^{M\times N}$ of $M$ \emph{source} models on every item.
We choose a sample $S$ of $n\ll N$ items using only $Y$, run the target on $S$ only, and output $\hat\mu$.
Quality is the error of $\hat\mu$ against the true $\mu$ (RMSE, MAE, signed bias) and how well the $\hat\mu$ of several targets orders them.
This is the estimation of the mean of a finite population of $N$ unknown values from $n$ observed ones, with a covariate known for all $N$ units, namely the columns of $Y$.
Seen this way, the source models can reduce the \emph{variance} of $\hat\mu$, through the choice of $S$ and through the estimator, while the \emph{bias} is controlled by how $S$ is drawn.

\paragraph{Target splits.}
Which models are targets relative to the sources matters, because a predictor fitted on the sources is only supported where the targets resemble them.
For each benchmark we use three protocols that differ only in how models are divided into sources and targets.
\textbf{Interpolation}: five random folds of the models; the targets are one fold and the sources the other four.
\textbf{Lineage-held-out}: the same, over model families rather than models, so that no target has a family member among the sources.
\textbf{Extrapolation}: the targets are the top 25\% of models by full score and the sources are the rest, so that every target scores above every source.
Families are derived from model names by keyword (Appendix~\ref{app:families}); the derivation is a heuristic.

\paragraph{Designs.}
A design draws $S$ of fixed size $n$ without replacement, with first-order inclusion probabilities $\pi_j$.
\emph{Uniform} sampling has $\pi_j=n/N$; \emph{stratified} sampling orders items by source difficulty and draws one item at random from each of $n$ consecutive blocks of $N/n$ items.
The \emph{PPS} design takes
\[
\pi_j \;=\; n\Big[(1-\varepsilon)\,\frac{w_j}{\sum_k w_k}+\frac{\varepsilon}{N}\Big],\qquad w_j=\sqrt{\hat p_j(1-\hat p_j)},
\]
where $\hat p_j$ is the fraction of sources answering item $j$ correctly (capped so that $\pi_j\le1$), drawn by systematic sampling in difficulty order.
It favours items on which the sources disagree, and the floor $\varepsilon n/N>0$ keeps every item, including those no source solves, drawable, which is what makes a design-based estimator unbiased whatever the target is.
The \emph{balanced} design selects greedily, from a random pool of $4n$ items, the $n$ whose mean reproduces the full scores of all sources.
\emph{Anchor} selection clusters the items by their source response vectors with $k$-means ($k=n$) and keeps the medoid of each cluster, weighted by cluster size~\citep{vivek2024anchor}.
\emph{Information-top} and \emph{CAT} designs choose the $n$ items of highest two-parameter-logistic (2PL) Fisher information, once for all targets or adaptively for each target.
Item selection and the hyperparameters $\varepsilon$ use sources only.

\paragraph{Predictors and estimators.}
A predictor $\hat p^{(y_S)}_j$ gives the probability that the target answers item $j$ correctly, given its answers $y_S$ on the sample and fitted on the sources.
We use a regression of full score on sample score across sources (\emph{calreg}), a 2PL item-response model with a latent ability fitted to the sample (\emph{IRT}), $k$ nearest sources by agreement on the sample (\emph{kNN}), and kernel ridge regression from sample responses to the full response vector (\emph{ridge}).
Four estimators combine a predictor with the sample.
The \emph{mean} estimator is the Hájek mean $\sum_{j\in S}y_j/\pi_j\big/\sum_{j\in S}1/\pi_j$ and ignores the predictor.
The \emph{model} estimator is $\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N\hat p_j$.

    if d == "anchor": return "anchor"
    if e.startswith("recal"): return "target-recalibrated"
    if e.startswith("diff-"): return "difference-corrected"
    if e in ("mean", "calreg"): return "design-based (mean, calreg)"
    return "model-based"

### Delivery

A push to your repository's `main`, or to `dev` of `paper-repo` (below), is a delivery; a local commit is not. A file over 20 MiB, and data files in bulk whatever their size (`*.npz`, `*.csv` and the like), go in Git LFS (`git lfs track '<pattern>'` before adding them). The roles you supply see the push among what changed around them, with your commit subjects where they read your code. The system records which revision of each repository the delivery comes from, so never write a commit's own SHA into its files.

The delivery is the repository of `paper-repo`, as a version takes it (`ht-role guide versions`). The roles integrate it on its `dev` branch: `paper-repo` and every role that reads its pull requests push their parts straight to `dev`, with no review. `dev` is not rewritten: rebase before you push. `.forgejo/CODEOWNERS` says who owns each path: change what is yours, and ask the owner for a change to what is not. Your next activation says who changed a path of yours. Close the request a push answers: that wakes the asker. A role that does not read the pull requests of `paper-repo` hands its part to a neighbor that does.

Only `paper-repo` pushes other branches there, and `main` takes pull requests only. To offer a version, `paper-repo` cuts `candidate-<name>` from `dev` and opens a pull request into `main`. The system asks the owners of the paths it changes to review it once, and their request for changes holds it; a fix to the candidate asks again only the owners of what it changes. Schedule the merge of a pull request you will merge yourself as soon as you open it: the approval that completes its reviews and checks does not wake you; a request for changes does, and so does an approval Forgejo cannot merge on.

Working material that stays in your repository outside the delivered paths (a diagnostic plot, notes) is yours; anything you put under a delivered path is a delivery. Only the world's required paths, the venue's declared paths and the files this contract names are fixed; other names, formats and layout are yours, so do not reshape the work to match a guessed filename.

`.forgejo/CODEOWNERS` in `paper-repo`'s repository records which role owns each delivered path, one regular expression of paths and its owners (`@<role>`) a line. A file you add under a path it already gives you is part of your delivery and needs no new line. `paper-repo` divides the work, so it owns the line `\.forgejo/CODEOWNERS @paper-repo`. SKIP=${SKIP:-}
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1

q=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$q"' EXIT

    esac

      run $b $s --draws 10 --d 2 --ngrid $n2 --designs uniform,strat,pps,balanced --no-cat --extra --out results/raw_extra/2pct >> "$q"

# Choosing items to predict a model's full-benchmark score: code and results

Code, protocol and result tables for the study of how to choose `n ≪ N` benchmark items for a target model and predict its full-benchmark score from the item-level results of other ("source") models. Thirteen binary item × model matrices (7 Open LLM Leaderboard v2, 6 HELM), three target splits (random models, held-out model families, models above every source), seven item-selection designs, about a hundred predictor/estimator combinations.

Contents

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `src/bpred/` | library: data loading and de-duplication (`data.py`), designs, predictors, estimators, adaptive CAT (`core.py`) |
| `scripts/` | experiments and analyses, numbered in execution order (below); `run_all.sh` runs everything on one machine |
| `PROTOCOL.md` | the protocol, written before any target was scored, with the log of later deviations |
| `RESULTS_SCHEMA.md` | every file in `results/`, its columns, and how to read a method name |
| `REPRODUCE.md` | commands, seeds, compute budget, script → table/figure map |
| `REPRO_NOTES.md` | disclosure of an exposure to reserved material (read it) |
| `results/` | all aggregate CSVs behind the paper's numbers (~8 MB); raw per-draw predictions are too large for the repository (see "Raw outputs") |

## Environment

Python 3.11; numpy 2.4.6, scipy 1.17.1, pandas 3.0.6, scikit-learn 1.9.1, torch 2.14.1 (CPU build), joblib 1.6.0, pyarrow 26.0.0 (`requirements.txt`). No GPU. The scripts set `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=OMP_NUM_THREADS=MKL_NUM_THREADS=1`; keep BLAS single-threaded (multi-threaded BLAS made the small eigen-decompositions 10× slower on a shared machine). Peak memory of one worker < 6 GB.

## Data

`scripts/00_download.sh` downloads the 13 score matrices and model lists from a public repository at a pinned commit (`55faff496947789f94e6b5908c77cbc3e84f81ad` of `socialfoundations/benchmark-prediction`; ~80 MB) into `data/raw/` and writes `SHA256SUMS`. The data are **not** bundled here. Only the binary item-level outcomes (and model names, used to derive families) are used; no benchmark text, no code of that repository. The source repository states an MIT licence; the licences of the benchmark datasets whose outcomes the matrices record (Open LLM Leaderboard v2 tasks, HELM scenarios) were not individually verified, which is one reason the matrices are fetched rather than redistributed. `python3 scripts/01_audit.py` writes the audit (`results/audit.csv`): models, duplicates dropped, constant items, families.

## Run

```
bash scripts/00_download.sh
python3 -I scripts/01_audit.py
bash scripts/run_all.sh 8            # 8 worker processes; all experiments and analyses, writes results/raw*/ and results/*.csv
```

`SKIP="extra inner50" bash scripts/run_all.sh 8` leaves out stages (`main variants msrc 2pct extra inner50 analyze`). Step by step: `python3 -I scripts/02_run.py BENCH SPLIT --draws 10 --d 2 --out results/raw` runs one (benchmark, split) cell (`BENCH` ∈ the 13 names, `SPLIT` ∈ `interp lineage extrap extrap10 extrap50`; `--ngrid N` runs a single budget, `--designs`, `--no-cat`, `--msrc M`, `--extra`, `--inner-frac F`, `--tag`: see the header of the script); then `03_analyze.py`, `04_msrc.py`, `05_bands.py`, `06_select.py` (usage in their headers). `scripts/pilot_d.py` is the source-only pilot that fixed the latent dimension d = 2 (`results/pilot_d.csv`).

Seeds: `BASE_SEED = 20261126` combined with the tuple (benchmark, split, fold, n, draw, design index); fold assignment uses seed 0; bootstraps use fixed seeds in the scripts. Re-running reproduces the pickles bit for bit on the same library versions and CPU architecture class; across machines expect differences at the 1e-6 level in individual predictions (torch/BLAS), none that change a reported digit in the summaries we compared.

- **Intervals.** Error bars are 95 % percentile intervals of a family bootstrap: within each benchmark the target model families (individual models for the random-fold split) are resampled with replacement, 2000 replicates, the same replicate for every method of a benchmark so that method-to-method ratios are paired; the aggregate is the geometric mean over benchmarks of the RMSE ratio. Intervals of "best method" rows are optimistic because the method was picked after the results; `results/selected.csv` gives the same classes with the representative chosen without the held-out benchmark.
- **Compute.** CPU only; single-threaded workers (1 CPU, < 6 GB each). Main + sensitivity-split runs 4.7 CPU-hours; the remaining stages are listed in `REPRODUCE.md`.
- **Licences.** The score matrices come from a public repository stated to be MIT-licensed (data not redistributed here); the underlying benchmarks' licences were not checked individually. No baseline code was reused: the `benchpred` package of that repository, and the baselines' own repositories, were not used; every method is implemented in `src/bpred`. The code in this directory is released under the MIT licence for review purposes.

#6 Target-recalibrated estimator and a prior-shrinkage check for the extrapolation question
State:   open
Author:  idea-repo

Request (idea → analysis): run one more estimator family, and check one possible artefact, because results-v1 leave the extrapolation question half-answered.

**Why.** In results-v1 (ccb6895), in extrapolation the source-tuned-λ difference estimator is shrunk (inner "targets" are not above the real ones), fixed λ=1 removes the bias but buys little over stratified sampling, and pure model-based predictors lose by bias. The Brief (rev 3, §3b) adds the one estimator that does not need the target to resemble the sources or any source-side tuning that mimics the outer split.

**1. Target-recalibrated regression estimator (Brief §3b), any design (uniform, strat, pps, balanced):**
- fit on the target's n answers, weighted LS with weights 1/π: y_i ~ β0 + β1·s_i (+ β2·p̂_i^{CF});
- s_i = logit of the source mean accuracy of item i (source-only); optional second feature p̂_i^{CF} = cross-fitted IRT prediction (5-fold over the sample, as for `diff-irt`); ridge-stabilised if needed at n=10–25, said in the notes;
- estimate = mean of the fitted values over all N items (equivalently ȳ_Hájek + (x̄_all − x̄_S)'β̂); predictions clipped to [0,1];
- no hyperparameter tuned on sources except what is already fixed (feature set chosen on the source-only inner split, and a single choice for all splits stated in advance).
- Report in the same tables as the other estimators: ratio to uniform and to strat at n=100 and n/N=2%, all five splits, signed bias per target, per-target bias/variance, so it enters the primary-endpoint family as a method class ("target-recalibrated"), with the "post-hoc best of a grid" caveat the outline already sets. Priority: extrap, extrap10, extrap50, then interp, lineage.

**2. A possible artefact in `irt-model`/`irt-plugin` in extrapolation (RMSE ≈ 1.5–2× uniform):** is the MAP ability estimate shrunk by its prior toward the source mean (and items no source solves have clamped difficulty)? A check: the same predictor with a flat/weak prior (ML ability, or prior variance ×10) on extrap, to say whether "model-based predictors are biased above the sources" is a property of model-based prediction or of that prior. If it is the prior, the paper should say so; a model-based baseline that ignores it is a weak comparator.

**3. Optional, lower priority (Brief §3c):** two-phase target-adaptive design (n/2 stratified, then n/2 with π ∝ √(p̂(θ̂)(1−p̂(θ̂))) plus floor, conditional π in the estimator) on the extrap splits only, paired with strat and pps at the same n. Skip if cost is a problem; say "not run".

What this serves: Brief C2 (does a bias-by-design correction repair extrapolation, at what cost) and C3 (what the sources can buy). Whatever the outcome, it is reported; if the recalibrated estimator is no better than `balanced|diffnaive-irt`, that is also a finding.

"""Fall-back rate of the target-recalibrated estimators (idea-repo#6): share of (draw, target) pairs for which the regression was replaced by the
Hajek mean (fewer than 3 sampled items of either class, or a rank-deficient weighted design).
usage: python3 -I scripts/08_recal.py RAWDIR OUT.csv [--two-pct]
Output rows: split, n (the actual n), design, estimator, bench, k_targets, rate (mean over folds, weighted by targets). The pickles keep one rate per
(design, estimator, target) averaged over draws (and over the pps epsilon variants)."""
import pickle, glob, os, sys, numpy as np, pandas as pd

raw, out = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
rows = []
for f in sorted(glob.glob(f"{raw}/*__*.pkl")):
    recs = pickle.load(open(f, "rb"))["records"]
    for r in recs:
        for k, v in r["diag"].items():
            if k.startswith("fb:"):
                _, dn, est = k.split(":", 2)
                rows.append(dict(split=r["split"], bench=r["bench"], fold=r["fold"], n=r["n"], design=dn, estimator=est, k=len(v), fb=float(v.sum())))
d = pd.DataFrame(rows)
g = d.groupby(["split", "bench", "n", "design", "estimator"]).agg(k_targets=("k", "sum"), fb=("fb", "sum")).reset_index()
g["rate"] = g.fb / g.k_targets
g.drop(columns="fb").to_csv(out, index=False)
print(g.groupby(["split", "estimator"]).apply(lambda x: (x.fb.sum() / x.k_targets.sum())).unstack().round(3).to_string())
E

Analysis → story. Answers to the open items of this request, with files (all committed in `world/experiment-repo` `main`, commit 4977245 and later; one correction at the end that changes wording you already have).

**Where things are**
- Secondary endpoint n/N = 2 %: `results/twopct/` (`primary.csv`, `primary_suite.csv`, `selected.csv`, `per_bench`, `ratio_by_n`, …); n is labelled `0` there, the real budget is `round(0.02·N)` (column `n_actual` in `per_bench`/`targets`). Three main splits only (interp, lineage, extrap); extrap10/extrap50 are not run at 2 %.
- LOBO-selected class representatives (chosen without the held-out benchmark): `results/selected.csv`, `results/twopct/selected.csv`; suites all/OLL/HELM in `primary_suite.csv`. Columns `split, cls, held_out, suite, baseline, chosen, ratio, ci_lo, ci_hi, n_bench` (rows with `held_out` empty are the pooled geometric means; the row with "k distinct, mode …" gives the number of different choices over the held-out benchmarks).
- Larger-gap nested split: `results/inner50/` (same schema as the main results).
- Source count: `results/msrc.csv` (M = 0 means all sources).
- Per-target bias: `bias2_unbiased` and `n_draws` columns of `per_bench.csv.gz` (n = 100). The high-R run (R = 100 at n = 100 for the non-adaptive designs) is queued; I report when it is analysed and until then the bias² column is the R = 10/40 one, corrected for the MC variance of the mean.
- Stronger anchor k-means (n_init 10, max_iter 300): `results/kmstrong.csv`.

**Results to take over (RMSE ratio to uniform|mean, geometric mean over non-thin benchmarks, 95 % family bootstrap; LOBO-selected representative per class)**

| class | n=100 interp | lineage | extrap | extrap10 | extrap50 | 2 % interp | lineage | extrap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| design-based (mean, calreg) | 0.71 | 0.73 | 0.77 | 0.76 | 0.83 | 0.58 | 0.60 | 0.75 |
| difference-corrected | 0.65 | 0.70 | 0.82 [0.79,0.83] | 0.70 | 0.95 | 0.54 | 0.57 | 0.73 |
| model-based | 0.65 | 0.69 | 0.84 | 0.75 | 1.21 | 0.54 | 0.56 | 0.83 |
| anchor | 0.72 | 0.79 | 1.01 | 1.00 | 1.34 | 0.51 | 0.54 | 0.81 |
| info/adaptive | 0.68 | 0.67 | 1.04 | 0.99 | 1.47 | 0.51 | 0.51 | 0.71 |

Ratios to `strat|mean` (second baseline): n = 100 extrap difference-corrected 0.96 [0.93,0.98], design-based 0.91; 2 % extrap difference-corrected 0.87 [0.83,0.89], design-based 0.90. So the extrapolation gain over stratified sampling is scale-dependent: small at n = 100, larger at 2 % (n = 2–30 on the 13 benchmarks).

**Validity points you should carry**
1. The representatives are chosen by leave-one-benchmark-out; the post-hoc best of ~100 methods is better (difference-corrected extrap 0.82 post-hoc vs the 0.82 selected at n = 100; at 2 % the selected class is 0.73 with pps|diff-ridge). The paper must say which is which.
2. "Model-based loses" holds for the pure model predictors with IRT (irt-model/irt-plugin), not for the class: `balanced|ridge-plugin` is 0.84 in extrap (0.65 interp). Please do not write the class loses by bias; at extrap50 it does (1.21).
3. Tuned λ is shrunk when the inner split resembles the sources. With the larger-gap inner split (`inner50`, inner held-out share 0.5) `balanced|diff-irt` is 0.763 in extrap vs 0.784 for the fixed λ = 1 and 0.772 for `balanced|calreg`: the repair works, the margin over calreg is ~1 %, inside the noise of the method choice.
4. Source count: with M = 10 sources the difference estimators are worse than uniform; the benefit needs enough sources (see msrc.csv).
5. A stronger anchor k-means moves a few per cent and does not change the conclusion (kmstrong.csv).

"""Anchor-design robustness: RMSE ratio to uniform|mean at n = 100 with the light k-means of the main runs (n_init 1, 25 iterations) against a
strong k-means (n_init 10, 300 iterations; BPRED_KMEANS=strong), per (benchmark, split) for the benchmarks run.

import pickle, glob, os, sys, numpy as np, pandas as pd

    def rmse(recs, m):
        e = [((r["preds"][m].astype(float) - r["true"][None]) ** 2).mean(0) for r in recs if r["n"] == 100]

    u = rmse(B, "uniform|mean")

All numbers are computed by `scripts/02_run.py` (experiments, raw predictions in `results/raw/*.pkl`, not committed) and `scripts/03_analyze.py` (tables below). Scores are fractions in [0,1]; multiply by 100 for points. Every row says its benchmark, split and n (items); N is in `per_bench.csv.gz`.

# Reproduction

Environment: Python 3.11, numpy 2.4.6, scipy 1.17.1, pandas 3.0.6, scikit-learn 1.9.1, torch 2.14.1 (CPU), joblib 1.6.0, pyarrow 26.0.0 (`requirements.txt`). BLAS single-threaded (set in the scripts). CPU only; each worker is one process with 1 CPU and < 6 GB.

## All at once
```
bash scripts/00_download.sh
python3 -I scripts/01_audit.py
bash scripts/run_all.sh 8       # 8 workers; SKIP="extra msrc ..." leaves stages out
```
`run_all.sh` runs the stages below in order (`main variants msrc 2pct extra inner50 kmstrong highR analyze`) with `xargs -P`; every stage writes its own raw directory, `analyze` writes the CSVs.

## Stages (what each runs, CPU time on the shared single-CPU workers we used)
| stage | command (per benchmark, split cell) | raw dir | CPU-h |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main` | `02_run.py BENCH {interp,lineage,extrap} --draws 10 --d 2` (n ∈ {10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400}, n ≤ N/2; 7 designs, ~100 method variants) | `results/raw` | 3.3 |
| `variants` | the same for `extrap10`, `extrap50` (top 10 % / 50 % as targets) | `results/raw` | 1.4 |
| `2pct` | `--ngrid n2` with `n2 = round(0.02 N)`; n/N = 2 % secondary endpoint | `results/raw_2pct` | 0.9 |
| `msrc` | `--ngrid 100 --designs uniform,strat,pps,balanced --no-cat --msrc M --tag _M{10,30,100}` (interp, extrap) | `results/raw_msrc` | 0.4 |
| `extra` | `--ngrid 100` and `--ngrid n2`, `--designs uniform,strat,pps,balanced --no-cat --extra` (target-recalibrated estimators `recal-*` and weak-prior IRT `irtw-*`) | `results/raw_extra/{n100,2pct}` | EXTRA_CPUH |
| `inner50` | extrap, n = 100, uniform/strat/pps/balanced, `--inner-frac 0.5 --tag _inner50` (larger-gap inner split for the tuning of λ) | `results/raw_inner50` | 0.1 |
| `kmstrong` | anchor design only, `BPRED_KMEANS=strong` (k-means n_init 10, 300 iterations instead of 1 / 25), n = 100, interp and extrap, 7 benchmarks | `results/raw_kmstrong` | 0.1 |
| `highR` | interp, extrap, n = 100, uniform/strat/pps/balanced, `--R 100 --tag _R100` (100 subset draws per fold; draws 0–9 equal the main run's) | `results/raw_highR` | HIGHR_CPUH |

The largest cells are `mmlu_pro`, `bbh`, `openllm_math` (up to ~25 min each in `main`). The Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks dominate the cost.

Seeds: `BASE_SEED = 20261126` combined with the tuple (benchmark, split, fold, n, draw, design index); fold assignment uses seed 0; bootstraps use fixed seeds in the analysis scripts. Reruns on the same machine reproduce the pickles; other CPUs/BLAS were not tested.

## Analyses
